units.text: INT. GHOSTS - CONTINUOUS

Ah, you are thinking of the possibility that--Alas! yes, family life is certainly not always so pure as it ought to be. But in such a case as you point to, one can never know--at least with any certainty. Here, on the other hand--that you, a mother, can think of letting your son--
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: But I cannot--I wouldn't for anything in the world; that is precisely what I am saying.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: No, because you are a "coward," as you put it. But if you were not a "coward," then--? Good God! a connection so shocking!
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: So far as that goes, they say we are all sprung from connections of that sort. And who is it that arranged the world so, Pastor Manders?
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Questions of that kind I must decline to discuss with you, Mrs. Alving; you are far from being in the right frame of mind for them. But that you dare to call your scruples "cowardly"--!
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: Let me tell you what I mean. I am timid and faint-hearted because of the ghosts that hang about me, and that I can never quite shake off.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: What do you say hangs about you?
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: Ghosts! When I heard Regina and Oswald in there, it was as though ghosts rose up before me. But I almost think we are all of us ghosts, Pastor Manders. It is not only what we have inherited from our father and mother that "walks" in us. It is all sorts of dead ideas, and lifeless old beliefs, and so forth. They have no vitality, but they cling to us all the same, and we cannot shake them off. Whenever I take up a newspaper, I seem to see ghosts gliding between the lines. There must be ghosts all the country over, as thick as the sands of the sea. And then we are, one and all, so pitifully afraid of the light.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Aha--here we have the fruits of your reading. And pretty fruits they are, upon my word! Oh, those horrible, revolutionary, free-thinking books!
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: You are mistaken, my dear Pastor. It was you yourself who set me thinking; and I thank you for it with all my heart.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: I!
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: Yes--when you forced me under the yoke of what you called duty and obligation; when you lauded as right and proper what my whole soul rebelled against as something loathsome. It was then that I began to look into the seams of your doctrines. I wanted only to pick at a single knot; but when I had got that undone, the whole thing ravelled out. And then I understood that it was all machine-sewn.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Softly, with emotion.
And was that the upshot of my life's hardest battle?
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: Call it rather your most pitiful defeat.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: It was my greatest victory, Helen--the victory over myself.
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: It was a crime against us both.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: When you went astray, and came to me crying, "Here I am; take me!" I commanded you, saying, "Woman, go home to your lawful husband." Was that a crime?
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: Yes, I think so.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: We two do not understand each other.
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: Not now, at any rate.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Never--never in my most secret thoughts have I regarded you otherwise than as another's wife.
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: Oh--indeed?
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Helen--!
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: People so easily forget their past selves.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: I do not. I am what I always was.
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: Changing the subject.
Well well well; don't let us talk of old times any longer. You are now over head and ears in Boards and Committees, and I am fighting my battle with ghosts, both within me and without.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Those without I shall help you to lay. After all the terrible things I have heard from you today, I cannot in conscience permit an unprotected girl to remain in your house.
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: Don't you think the best plan would be to get her provided for?--I mean, by a good marriage.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: No doubt. I think it would be desirable for her in every respect. Regina is now at the age when--Of course I don't know much about these things, but--
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: Regina matured very early.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Yes, I thought so. I have an impression that she was remarkably well developed, physically, when I prepared her for confirmation. But in the meantime, she ought to be at home, under her father's eye--Ah! but Engstrand is not--That he--that he--could so hide the truth from me!
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: A knock at the door into the hall.
Who can this be? Come in!
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: In his Sunday clothes, in the doorway.
I humbly beg your pardon, but--
units.name: ENGSTRAND

units.text: Aha! H'm--
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: Is that you, Engstrand?
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: --there was none of the servants about, so I took the great liberty of just knocking.
units.name: ENGSTRAND

units.text: Oh, very well. Come in. Do you want to speak to me?
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Comes in.
No, I'm obliged to you, ma'am; it was with his Reverence I wanted to have a word or two.
units.name: ENGSTRAND

units.text: Walking up and down the room.
Ah--indeed! You want to speak to me, do you?
units.name: MANDERS
